CaseCauseConscienceKyle

The Cause · Immediate cause

A defeat device: software built to recognise a test

In a lab test, the software watched for…

Steering wheel not turning

Speed follows the test pattern

How long the engine has run

Air pressure

Is this a test?

YES

NO

Controls fully ON

→ the car passes the test

Controls turned DOWN

→ it pollutes on real roads

Nothing broke: the cheating was the design itself.

Why

did engineers choose to build it this way?

Source: US EPA notice of violation (18 Sept. 2015), via E&E News; Congressional Research Service (2015). Illustration by the group.

CaseCauseConscienceLucy

The Cause · Contributing cause

Volkswagen set up the conditions for cheating

Ambition

No. 1

carmaker in the world: the goal

Grow fast in the US with “clean diesel”

+

Low budget

EU limit

US limit

4× stricter

Cleaner tech cost more, and was not funded

+

Top-down culture

Targets from the top; failure not accepted

=

Result

Cheating becomes likely

Hard target, small budget, no one to stop it

Sources: IHS Automotive (2015), NOx limits for the EA189 engine: EU 0.18 g/km, US 0.044 g/km; US EPA

CaseCauseConscienceLucy

The Cause · Judgement cause

Around 2006, engineers chose to hide the problem

2006

The problem

The engine could not meet US limits

Option A

Tell the truth

Option B · their choice

Hide it with software

Kept for almost

10 years

Engineers objected in 2006. The project went ahead.

Source: US Department of Justice, Volkswagen Statement of Facts (2017)

The Conscience · Pressure

Three pressures pushed the engineers toward the cheat

1

2

3

the cheat

Cost

No budget for the honest solution

Orders

“…not to get caught”

a manager, late 2006

Secrecy

Silence felt like loyalty

Pressure explains behaviour. It does not justify it.

Source: US Department of Justice, Volkswagen Statement of Facts (2017)

CaseCauseConscienceKinsen

The Conscience · Rules

Loyalty was a duty, but deeper rules outweighed it

Loyalty

WFEO 1.3

Good faith towards the employer

outweighed by

Public safety comes first

WFEO 4.3

Protect public health and the environment

ACM 1.03

Software must not harm the public

HKIE

Safeguard public safety and health

Loyalty is conditional. Public safety is paramount.

Sources: WFEO Model Code of Ethics; ACM/IEEE-CS Software Engineering Code; HKIE Rules of Conduct

CaseCauseConsciencePeter

The Conscience · Comparison

Protecting the public outweighs loyalty to the employer

Loyalty to the employer
WFEO 1.3

Public health and environment
WFEO 4.3

1

Loyalty has limits

Good faith never covers fraud

2

The public had no defence

Only the engineers knew

3

It did not even help Volkswagen

It cost the company €30 billion+

CaseCauseConsciencePeter

The Conscience · Requirement

Acting ethically meant saying no, at a personal cost

Step 1

Refuse

to write the code

Step 2

Tell the truth

to their managers

Step 3

Report it

to the authorities

The cost

Projects

Promotions

Even their jobs

That is the price engineers must be ready to pay.

CaseCauseConsciencePeter

The Conscience · Judgement

Ethical only to a very limited extent

Unethical

Ethical

In their favour

Met the targets

Under real pressure

Against them

Not honest

Put public health at risk

Hid it for almost 10 years

They kept the smaller duty and broke the greater one. Our verdict: unethical.

Conclusion

Engineering ethics is about how we behave when nobody is testing us.

The student

fools one teacher

Volkswagen’s engineers

fooled regulators worldwide, and the public paid the price

Seminar discussion · Question 1

Who is more to blame?

The engineers, or the test that was easy to fool?

TEST

the easy way round

A

The engineers

In this case: they knew the rules, and broke them anyway.

or

B

The test

In this case: it was so easy to fool, it gave them the chance.

Seminar discussion · Question 2

Who is more responsible: Volkswagen’s company culture, or the engineers who made and kept the cheating software?

Company culture

The engineers

?

Led by Kinsen

Seminar discussion · Question 3

Research: people given specific targets are more likely to behave unethically than people told to “do their best”.

Does that make VW’s management responsible, or does it excuse the engineers?

Source: Schweitzer, Ordóñez & Douma, “Goal setting as a motivator of unethical behavior”, Academy of Management Journal (2004)
